questions.prompt: Hicks’s motivational thesis at the start of Logic is best captured by which claim?
choices: A Logic is impractical except as a puzzle game.
B For humans, mastering logic is the most practical mastery available.
C Physical speed matters more than mental method.
D Aristotle forbade calling logic a tool.
questions.explain: He calls logic the most practical thing one can master.

questions.prompt: “Organon” in this course refers to:
choices: B Aristotle’s logic books, named with the Greek for tool.
C A medieval tax on monks.
questions.explain: Collectively Aristotle’s logic writings: tools of thinking.

questions.prompt: Non-contradiction, in the formulation Hicks quotes, forbids:
choices: A Using more than one premise.
B The same attribute belonging and not belonging to the same subject at once in the same respect.
questions.explain: Metaphysics: not both F and not-F of the same subject, same time, same respect.

questions.prompt: Logicians, unlike a shouting match, require an argument to include:
choices: A A conclusion plus premise(s) as reasons.
B Only insults ranked by volume.
questions.explain: Conclusion = what to believe; premises = why.

questions.prompt: If premises match the facts but the inference is a non sequitur, Hicks would say the argument fails on:
choices: A Truth of the components only.
B Validity (form), even if some statements are true.
questions.explain: True bits can still be invalidly combined; validity is structural.

questions.prompt: Hicks quotes Voltaire on long arguments among the enlightened to highlight:
choices: A That wit replaces conceptual clarity.
B The risk that the question itself is unclear.
C That sensations are already theories.
D That children cannot form percepts.
questions.explain: Fuzzy questions and equivocal words are an occupational hazard.

questions.prompt: Percepts stand in the hierarchy as:
choices: A Integrations of sensations into object-awareness.
B The same thing as axioms of logic.
questions.explain: Sensations are bundled into percepts of objects.

questions.prompt: A toddler saying “dog” of several different animals is, for Hicks, using:
questions.explain: Not one percept’s name—an open class.

questions.prompt: Counting a hen’s speckles illustrates that:
choices: A Perception already includes exact cardinality.
B Number is a learned conceptual overlay, not a better look.
D Concepts are innate at birth as full arithmetic.
questions.explain: You still see the hen the same; 872 is conceptual.

questions.prompt: Before debating “Does God exist?” or “Is he a socialist?”, Hicks wants you first to:
choices: B Clarify the concepts in play.
D Shift the burden of proof.
questions.explain: Univocal concepts first, then arguments.

questions.prompt: Informal fallacies are “informal” here mainly because they:
choices: B Crop up across many reasoning forms, not just one formal pattern.
C Are officially valid in the Organon.
questions.explain: Common bad patterns wherever you reason, not one specialized calculus.

questions.prompt: Turning up the car radio so you won’t hear a bad engine noise is Hicks’s comic case of:
choices: B Subjectivism: not wanting the problem, so treating it as absent.
questions.explain: Policy of not wanting there to be engine trouble, so drowning the evidence.

questions.prompt: “Lots of people believe X, so X” is the fallacy of:
questions.explain: Others’ belief isn’t by itself your evidence.

questions.prompt: Dismissing Nietzsche’s arguments because “he went crazy” is offered as:
choices: B Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the arguments.
C Begging the question by restatement.
questions.explain: Later madness is treated as refuting earlier arguments that stand or fall on their own.

questions.prompt: Asch-style line experiments are brought in to illuminate why people fall for:
choices: B Majority/conformity pressure even against what they can see.
questions.explain: Subjects often match the planted majority against visible differences.

questions.prompt: If your premise already contains the conclusion, Hicks’s name for the defect is:
questions.explain: You assumed what you set out to prove.

questions.prompt: Redefining “Buddhist” as “whoever is virtuous,” then denying Singh is a Buddhist because he isn’t virtuous, is:
choices: B Question-begging by substituting a loaded definition.
D Induction from a pasta pot.
questions.explain: Ordinary marks of being a Buddhist are replaced so the thesis can’t lose.

questions.prompt: You vouch for your friend who vouches for you to a banker. This models:
choices: A Circular reasoning with no independent check.
questions.explain: Each supports the other; the officer has no outside verification.

questions.prompt: “Have you stopped beating your spouse?”-type traps are classified as:
questions.explain: Yes and no each concede part of a smuggled pair of claims.

questions.prompt: “Prove that God does not exist, or my theism stands” is criticized as:
choices: A Proper placement of the burden on the existence-claimant.
B Illegitimate burden-shifting / appeal to ignorance.
D A truth table with 16 rows.
questions.explain: The existence claim carries the initial evidential burden.

questions.prompt: How many premises does a syllogism have in this course’s usage?
choices: D Zero if it is sound.
questions.explain: Two premises and a conclusion; three families of syllogism.

questions.prompt: True premises plus a conclusion that does not follow yields:
questions.explain: Good information, botched reasoning: unsound.

questions.prompt: The medieval mnemonic Hicks mentions for the all-all-all valid mood is:
questions.explain: That pattern is named Barbara—always valid as a form.

questions.prompt: Soundness requires:
choices: B True premises and valid form together.
C False premises and valid form only.
D Valid form regardless of truth, called “sound” anyway.
questions.explain: Neither virtue alone is enough; both make a sound argument.

questions.prompt: The middle term is the category that:
choices: A Shows up in both premises as the link.
D Is the same as a consequent.
questions.explain: It is the term common to the two premises.

questions.prompt: The consequent of an if-then is:
questions.explain: After “then”; the if-clause is the antecedent.

questions.prompt: Modus ponens is another name for:
questions.explain: Valid mixed form: affirm the if-clause, draw the then-clause.

questions.prompt: “If you insult him he’ll be angry; he is angry; so you insulted him” is:
questions.explain: Anger has many causes; the consequent doesn’t uniquely prove the antecedent.

questions.prompt: No oxygen, therefore no fire—given “if fire then oxygen”—is:
questions.explain: Second premise denies the then-clause; fire is ruled out. Modus tollens.

questions.prompt: A pure hypothetical syllogism (“chain”) stays in if-then throughout and concludes by linking:
choices: A The first antecedent to the last consequent.
B Two middle terms in predicate position.
C A celebrity to a product.
questions.explain: First if-clause chained through to the final then-clause.

questions.prompt: Inclusive disjunction P v Q is true when:
choices: B At least one disjunct is true.
C The argument is an ad hominem.
questions.explain: Fill the truth table: true if one or both sides hold.

questions.prompt: “If and only if” is unpacked as:
choices: A Two hypotheticals: P→Q and Q→P.
C Denying both antecedent and consequent.
questions.explain: Biconditional = both directions of if-then.

questions.prompt: Constructive dilemma combines an either-or with:
choices: C A Venn diagram of three circles only.
questions.explain: Each disjunct has an if-then; you exit with a disjunction of consequents.

questions.prompt: Hicks connects propositional T/F to computing by noting that:
choices: A Hegel already built the first chip.
B On/off switches can instantiate binary 1/0 as truth-values.
C Informal fallacies cannot be symbolized even in principle.
questions.explain: Electrical on/off maps onto the logical binary, enabling circuits.

questions.prompt: A short proof using MT then disjunctive syllogism (the Rochester/Toronto style reconstruction) shows that:
choices: A Truth tables are the only legitimate method.
B Named valid patterns can extract hidden conclusions more economically than brute tables.
C Chain arguments are always invalid.
D Burden of proof always sits on the denier.
questions.explain: Modus tollens knocks out T; remaining disjunct R follows—creative use of stored valid forms.

questions.prompt: Induction, contrasted with the fuchsia/chlorophyll deduction, starts from:
choices: A A universal already in hand.
B Particulars, then generalizes to a wider class.
C An insult to a speaker.
questions.explain: 280 liars → claim about chronic liars as a class.

questions.prompt: Tasting one noodle and judging the pot is Hicks’s everyday picture of:
choices: B Inductive generalization from a particular.
questions.explain: You don’t test each piece; you generalize—then he warns about bad generalizations.

questions.prompt: Walking under a ladder then twisting an ankle is a cautionary case of:
questions.explain: One coincidence treated as cause—induction gone off the rails.

questions.prompt: Hicks’s methodological moral about inductive confidence is:
choices: A Demand the same necessity you get in deduction, immediately.
B Allow cautious, increasing generalization rather than instant certainty.
D Treat all induction as informal fallacies.
questions.explain: Certainty isn’t the right immediate standard for all inductive work.

questions.prompt: Semmelweis noticing matching symptoms in a colleague is an example of:
choices: A Closed deduction with no new observation.
B Discovery that feeds and revises an observational/conceptual scheme.
C Appeal to majority among priests.
D Shifting the burden of proof about God.
questions.explain: New observation (Kolletschka) inside categories already in play, opening the next hypothesis.
